teachingNote:
Orange mushroom, hymenium running down the stem, autumn woods. Nearly everything a beginner reaches for here is shared by all three species, which is why this set is the first one.

What does not separate them: all three run their spore-bearing surface down the stem, so 'decurrent' proves nothing. All three drop a whitish print, so the spore print — the technique that saves you from a destroying angel — is useless here. All three cut solid, and all three discolour brownish when handled.

What does separate them: the Appalachian chanterelle has false ridges, blunt and forking and continuous with the cap flesh; the jack-o'-lantern has true gills, thin and sharp-edged and separable. Both chanterelles come up alone or scattered from soil, mycorrhizal with oak and beech, and smell of apricot; the jack-o'-lantern comes up in dense clusters with fused bases from hardwood and smells of nothing.

The smooth chanterelle is here to break the rule before it hardens. Its hymenium is smooth to shallowly wrinkled — neither ridges nor gills — so a player who has learned 'ridges good, gills bad' meets a chanterelle with neither and has to fall back on habit, substrate and odor. That is the transferable skill: characters are evidence, not rules.

It also means the two chanterelles differ in exactly one reachable character. On an individual whose underside cannot be read — a weathered specimen, or one found off its substrate — they are genuinely indistinguishable, and declining is the full-credit answer. That is correct, and it is not a gap in the data.

The substrate check has a trap in it. Jack-o'-lanterns fruit from buried roots, so a cluster can appear to rise straight out of bare ground. Growth habit is what rescues you: fused at the base means wood, whatever the surface says. That is why the set carries both characters instead of one.

Odor is the most fragile of the five and the game should treat it that way — rain takes it out, and an individual with weathering above 0.4 will not give it up at all.
